title: Bronchial Asthma: Systemic & Ocular Perspectives
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to bronchial asthma, focusing on the GINA-aligned management protocols, underlying pathophysiology, and the critical ocular associations including atopic disease and steroid-induced complications.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Bronchial asthma is a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by a history of respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough that vary over time and in intensity, together with variable expiratory airflow limitation. From an ophthalmic perspective, it is frequently associated with atopic ocular surface diseases (AKC/VKC).

content.explanation: Aspirin Exacerbated Respiratory Disease consists of: 1. Asthma, 2. Sinusitis/Nasal Polyps, 3. Aspirin/NSAID Sensitivity.

sections.title: Ocular Associations & Manifestations
content: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis (AKC): Chronic, bilateral, potentially blinding inflammation.
Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC): Seasonal, giant papillae (cobblestones), Horner-Trantas dots.
Keratoconus: High association due to chronic eye rubbing (itch-scratch cycle).
Steroid-Induced Glaucoma: Secondary to chronic systemic or inhaled corticosteroid use.
Posterior Subcapsular Cataracts (PSC): Common side effect of long-term ICS or systemic prednisone.
Allergic Conjunctivitis: Frequently co-exists with allergic asthma and rhinitis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Spirometry: Demonstrate reversible airflow obstruction (FEV1 increase >12% and >200mL).
2. Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) Monitoring: Diurnal variability >10%.
3. Bronchial Provocation: Methacholine or Histamine challenge (PC20 < 8mg/mL).
4. Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO): Marker of eosinophilic inflammation.
5. Allergy Testing: Skin prick tests or Specific IgE.

rows: Inspiratory stridor; flattened inspiratory loop on spirometry
Basal crackles; orthopnea; B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP) elevated
Acute onset; pleuritic chest pain; normal spirometry
Add LAMA; Add Biologic (Anti-IgE, Anti-IL5, Anti-IL4R); Consider OCS

sections.title: Red Flags: Status Asthmaticus
content: Silent Chest (Ominous sign of minimal air movement)
Cyanosis or SpO2 < 90% on room air
Altered Mental Status (Confusion or exhaustion)
Inability to speak in full sentences
Paradoxical Thoraco-abdominal breathing
Normal or elevated PaCO2 (Indicates impending respiratory failure)

sections.title: Biologic Therapies (Precision Medicine)
content: Omalizumab: Anti-IgE (For severe allergic asthma).
Mepolizumab/Reslizumab: Anti-IL5 (For eosinophilic asthma).
Benralizumab: Anti-IL5 Receptor α.
Dupilumab: Anti-IL4/IL13 (Also used for severe Atopic Dermatitis).
Tezepelumab: Anti-TSLP (Targets upstream epithelial cytokines).

sections.title: Ocular Side Effects of Asthma Tx
content: Inhaled Corticosteroids (ICS): Risk of Ocular Hypertension/Glaucoma if technique is poor (facial deposition).
Systemic Corticosteroids: Highest risk for PSC Cataracts and Glaucoma.
Antimuscarinic agents (LAMA/SAMA): May trigger Acute Angle Closure in susceptible narrow angles.
Dupilumab: Frequently causes Conjunctivitis and Blepharitis as a side effect (10-25%).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: A normal CXR does not rule out asthma; it is usually normal or shows hyperinflation.
Avoid Beta-Blockers (even topical Timolol) in asthmatics as they can trigger fatal bronchospasm.
The 'Asthmatic Eye': Always check IOP and lens clarity in patients on long-term steroid therapy.
Charcot-Leyden crystals and Curschmann spirals are classic pathology findings in sputum.
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB) peaks 5-10 minutes after stopping exercise.

rows: PRN ICS-formoterol is superior to SABA alone for symptom control and exacerbation reduction.
Addition of LAMA to ICS/LABA improves lung function in uncontrolled asthma.
ICS improves airway hyperresponsiveness but does not prevent lung function decline over time.
